sections.h2: Where are Lake County, Florida property records kept?
sections.html:
Lake County deeds, mortgages and liens are kept by the Lake County Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller in the Official Records. The clerk's recording section handles deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, liens, powers of attorney, notices of commencement, agreements for deed, plats, judgments, financing statements and death certificates.

The clerk's site describes the office as the keeper of the county's Official Records. That site has a records search area, a page on researching Official Records, and a tax deed record search. The Property Appraiser keeps the parcel and ownership side, so a full picture of a house means checking both offices.

  • Clerk: recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, lis pendens, tax deed files.
  • Property Appraiser: parcel data, owner of record on the tax roll, exemptions.
  • Tax Collector: tax bills and any certificate on the parcel.

sections.h2: How much does recording cost at the Lake County clerk?
sections.html:
The Lake County clerk's recording fee page prints $10.00 for the first page of an instrument up to 8.5 by 14 inches and $8.50 for each additional page. Indexing adds $1.00 for each name over four.

The statute behind these amounts, section 28.24(13), sets a base of $5.00 for a first page and $4.00 for each added page, plus separate modernization and technology charges. The clerk's printed totals are the amounts to budget. The clerk's page also links a fee calculator for deeds and mortgages.

sections.h2: What taxes does the clerk collect when a Lake County deed is recorded?
sections.html:
The clerk collects documentary stamp tax on the deed at recording. The clerk's page gives the deed rate as 70 cents per $100 of consideration or fraction thereof, with a minimum of 70 cents on deeds whose consideration is $100 or less.

Florida's Department of Revenue explains that all parties to a document are liable for the tax whichever one agrees to pay, and that deeds are taxable whether recorded or not. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable, while quit claim and special warranty deeds, contracts for deed and deeds in lieu of foreclosure are listed as taxable.

Mortgages carry two charges at recording, according to the clerk's page: documentary stamps of 35 cents per $100 on the promise to pay, and a one-time intangible tax of 2 mills, which is .002 per $1. A seller using a cash buyer with no new loan usually sees only the deed stamps, so ask the title company what is being recorded.

sections.h2: How do you get a document recorded in Lake County?
sections.html:
Every document goes through the clerk's Recording Section, and the clerk says four methods are available: in person, by mail, by drop box and by eRecording. The page states documents are recorded in order received, typically within two business days, and that same-day or next-day recording cannot be guaranteed for mail, drop box or electronic submissions.

If timing matters, the clerk recommends recording in person at one of its two locations. Checks are payable to the clerk and comptroller, and the page says cashier's checks dated more than two months before are not accepted. Cards from Visa, MasterCard, Discover and American Express are taken, and a non-refundable processing fee applies to card payments.

  • Include an "this instrument prepared by" statement, which Florida law requires on the face of conveyances.
  • Use the clerk's Recording Transmittal Form to speed processing.
  • Leave out Social Security numbers unless the law requires them.
  • Expect the recorded document back by U.S. first class mail, with an envelope optional.

sections.h2: Can a Lake County owner watch for fraudulent deeds?
sections.html:
Yes. The Property Appraiser's home page describes a free Clerk of the Court service that sends an email when a document is recorded under a monitored name, and it allows up to five names for each registered email address.

The page notes that scammers file false deeds to look like owners and then collect money for rentals or sales. Owners of vacant, inherited or out-of-state houses are the most exposed, because nobody is watching the mailbox. Sign up through the clerk's recording notification service, and check the Official Records search yourself now and then for your surname.

Recording order matters. The clerk records documents in the order received, so a deed and the mortgage that funds it should arrive together, and the closing agent usually sends them the same day.

sections.h2: What should a Lake County seller check in the records before listing?
sections.html:
Pull the vesting deed and look for open mortgages, judgments, liens and a lis pendens, because each one has to be paid or released before a buyer gets clear title. A title company runs this search at closing, but running it first avoids surprises.

  • The deed names exactly who owns the house and how they hold title.
  • Any mortgage without a recorded satisfaction.
  • Notices of commencement or liens from contractors.
  • A lis pendens, which signals a lawsuit tied to the parcel.
  • Prior-year tax certificates, checked with the tax collector.

For an inherited house, ask the clerk's probate section what must be on file before the personal representative can sign a deed. Florida's list of taxable deeds does not include a personal representative's deed under a probated will, which is a useful point to raise with your closing agent.

sections.h2: How do lis pendens and foreclosure show up in Lake County records?
sections.html:
A foreclosure lawsuit announces itself in the Official Records through a lis pendens, which the clerk records for $5.00 on the first page and $4.00 for each added page. Release of one costs $10.00 and $8.50 under the clerk's fee page.

Under Florida's statute for judicial sales, a final judgment directs the clerk to sell the property at public sale not less than 20 days or more than 35 days after judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to longer. Notice runs for two consecutive weeks, and the high bidder leaves a 5 percent deposit. Lake County's clerk keeps a foreclosure sales calendar on its site, which is the place to confirm any sale date. A homeowner who sees a lis pendens against the house should talk to a Florida attorney and can still sell before the sale if the payoff is covered.

faqs.q: Does the Lake County clerk record deeds?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk of the circuit court is the county recorder and keeps deeds, mortgages, liens and other instruments in the Official Records. Recording happens in the clerk's Recording Section.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Lake County?
faqs.a: The clerk's page prints $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, plus $1.00 for each name beyond four. Documentary stamp tax on the deed is separate, at 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

faqs.q: How long does Lake County recording take?
faqs.a: The clerk says documents are recorded in order received, typically within two business days. Same-day recording is not guaranteed for mail, drop box or eRecording, so record in person if the date matters.

faqs.q: Can I record a Lake County document electronically?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk lists eRecording as one of four ways to record, along with in person, mail and drop box.

faqs.q: Is there a free alert for new documents on my Lake County property?
faqs.a: Yes. The Clerk of the Court offers a free email notice when a document is recorded under a monitored name, with up to five names per email address, as described on the Property Appraiser's home page.
